# North York Moors National Park

Scroll down


## Perfect days, starry nights

**Make magical memories in a peaceful corner of northern England.**

Sweeping moorland, a crinkly coast, ancient woods and timeless villages – the North York Moors is a special place, forged by nature and shaped over generations. Give yourself time to discover its secrets, from amazing wildlife to dazzling night skies.

## Special qualities

Overview

The North York Moors is a special place – here’s why!

Our wildlife will surprise you – from the moorland merlin, the UK’s smallest bird of prey, to whales off the North York Moors coast.

The North York Moors has vast areas of clear, dark skies – you can often see up to 2,000 stars, including a swathe of our own galaxy, the Milky Way.

There’s history and heritage in every step you take, from Gothic ruins to Victorian steam trains, Cistercian monasteries to stately homes, ironstone mines to fishing villages. The National Park also features over 800 Scheduled Monuments and 1,500 ancient boundary stones and crosses.

Our 44,000 hectares of heather moorland are designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest for its heathland habitat and breeding birds, such as red grouse, curlew and golden plover.

There are 26 miles of Jurassic-era coastline to explore, including the famous old fishing villages of Staithes and Robin Hood’s Bay.

You could walk or cycle every day for a year and still not cover every corner of the National Park – there are 2,250 kilometres of rights of way alone, not to mention country lanes, quiet backroads, coastal tracks, forest trails and a National Trail.

## Did you know?

We’re not just moorland and coast – shady woodland covers around 23% of the National Park.

# Welcome to the North York Moors

The North York Moors was established as National Park in 1952 – a treasured landscape in the heart of North Yorkshire, protected for everyone to enjoy. We cover 1,436 square kilometres between Scarborough, Thirsk and Teesside.

Of the 1,500 ancient boundary stones and crosses here, probably the most famous is Young Ralph Cross, adopted as the National Park’s distinctive logo. We like to think that this stone cross on the spreading moorland stands for a state of mind – this wonderful landscape, it’s saying, is somewhere to come and refresh your spirits. It’s the place where magical things happen – where the stresses and strains of daily life disappear, and where relaxation, holidays and adventure begin.

Discover the places and meet the people to take you on this journey. Experience the very best of the North York Moors and forge lasting memories with family and friends. Join wildlife experts from Yorkshire Coast Nature and set sail from Staithes in search of Minke whales. Smell the myriad of sweet scents at Helmsley Walled Garden, featured in the 2020 film adaptation of The Secret Garden. Taste your way through delicacies from our moorland and coast – whether it’s kippers from Fortune’s, Whitby’s traditional smokehouse or a jar of Westfield honey from hives set amongst the heather around Fadmoor. Find your inner peace with Adventures for the Soul who teach the practice of mindfulness whilst out in nature.

The open moorland – ablaze with purple heather in summer – will give you a rare sense of space. Away from the noise of traffic, you can hear the cries of moorland birds, the trickling water in a stream and the buzz of insects in the heather. On the coast, experience the roar of the sea, the wind in your hair, the sand between your toes. The dales form a rich patchwork of earthy colours, hedgerows and drystone walls – landscapes, created generations ago, still maintained by today’s farmers. Our woodlands and ancient trees provide a sense of well-being and a link to the past. And far from the artificial lights of towns, there are truly dark skies where you can see majestic skyscapes full of stars. The North York Moors – it’s where we want you to feel at home.

![Columbia working with Camphill Community](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Columbia-working-with-Camphill-Community-by-Ben-Read-Photography-resized-1800x1080.jpg)
Columbia working with Camphill Community

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Yorkshire-Coastliner-840-bus-arriving-in-Goathland-village-Credit-rjbphotographic.co_.uk-resized-580x580.jpg)

### Getting around

The delightful Esk Valley Railway (Middlesbrough to Whitby) passes through the heart of the National Park; while the North Yorkshire Moors Railway runs steam heritage services from Pickering to Whitby. Or enjoy a ride on Coastliner 840 from York – voted Britain’s most scenic bus route!

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Greener-Travel_Esk-Valley-Railway-resized-580x580.jpg)

### Getting there

We’re closer than you think! Rail services and long-distance buses from across the country run to surrounding towns – and London to York can take less than two hours by train. Local bus links get you to scenic spots like Pickering, Helmsley, Goathland, Robin Hood’s Bay and Thornton le Dale.

# Welcome to the   North York Moors National Park

## A special place of great beauty and tranquillity

### Autumn, Blow Gill (c) Matt Hillier

**Langdale Forest & Fylingdales Moor restoration updates (autumn 2026)**

Open Access and Public Rights of Way are open, however the landscape across Fylingdales Moor remains vulnerable to further damage and erosion. Visitors are asked to follow any advisory signage and remain on designated paths, helping to protect public safety and support long-term environmental recovery. Please [visit our wildfire page](https://www.northyorkmoors.org.uk/climate-change/wildfire "Fylingdales Moor wildfire updates") to read all guidance and the latest updates as restoration work continues.

North York Moors National Park
sign near [Great Ayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ayton "Great Ayton") | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/North_York_Moors_map_en.png/330px-North_York_Moors_map_en.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:North_York_Moors_map_en.png) | | Location | North Yorkshire, England | | Area | 1,436km2 (554sqmi)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-DOI-1) | | Established | 1952 | | Governingbody | North York Moors National Park Authority | | Website | [www.northyorkmoors.org.uk](http://www.northyorkmoors.org.uk/) | The **North York Moors** is an upland area and [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_the_United_Kingdom "National parks of the United Kingdom") in [North Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Yorkshire "North Yorkshire"), England. It contains the largest expanse of [heather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calluna "Calluna") [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") in the United Kingdom. The area was designated a national park in 1952, through the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949 "National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949"). The park covers an area of 1,436km2 (554sqmi), and had a population of 22,935 at the [2021 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932022_United_Kingdom_censuses "2021–2022 United Kingdom censuses").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-2) It is administered by the North York Moors National Park Authority, which is based in [Helmsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmsley "Helmsley").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-3) ## Location and transport \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_York_Moors&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Location and transport")\] To the east, the area is clearly defined by the impressive cliffs of the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea") coast. The northern and western boundaries are defined by the steep scarp slopes of the [Cleveland Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Hills "Cleveland Hills") edging the Tees lowlands and the [Hambleton Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hambleton_Hills "Hambleton Hills") above the [Vale of Mowbray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vale_of_Mowbray "Vale of Mowbray"). To the south lies the broken line of the [Tabular Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabular_Hills "Tabular Hills") and the [Vale of Pickering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vale_of_Pickering "Vale of Pickering"). Four roads cross the North York Moors from north to south. In the east, the [A171](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A171_road "A171 road") joins [Whitby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitby "Whitby") and [Scarborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough,_North_Yorkshire "Scarborough, North Yorkshire"). Further inland, the [A169](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A169_road "A169 road") runs between [Pickering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickering,_North_Yorkshire "Pickering, North Yorkshire") and Whitby. More centrally, a minor road departs from the [A170](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A170_road "A170 road") at [Keldholme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keldholme?action=edit&redlink=1 "Keldholme (page does not exist)") and passes through [Castleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castleton,_North_Yorkshire "Castleton, North Yorkshire") before joining the A171 which connects Whitby and [Guisborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guisborough "Guisborough"). The most westerly route is the [B1257](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B1257_road "B1257 road") connecting [Helmsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmsley "Helmsley") to [Stokesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokesley "Stokesley"). The A170 from Thirsk to Scarborough marks the southern boundary of the North York Moors area. The [Esk Valley Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esk_Valley_Line "Esk Valley Line") is an east–west branch line rail link from Whitby to [Middlesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesbrough "Middlesbrough") in the north, and the [North Yorkshire Moors steam railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYMR "NYMR") runs from Pickering to Grosmont with a link to Whitby.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-4) Other public transport within the North York Moors includes a number of bus services. [Yorkshire Coastliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Coastliner "Yorkshire Coastliner") route 840 runs from Whitby to Pickering (and continues to York and Leeds), [Arriva North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arriva_North_East "Arriva North East") routes X93 and X94 run from Scarborough to Middlesbrough via Whitby and Guisborough, Arriva North East route 95 runs from Whitby to [Lealholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lealholm "Lealholm") along the Esk Valley, and [East Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Yorkshire_(bus_company) "East Yorkshire (bus company)") route 128 connects Scarborough and Helmsley. On weekends during the summer, these are complemented by [Moorsbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorsbus "Moorsbus") services, which run from local urban centres into more remote parts of the national park which are difficult to access without private transport. Some of the routes across the North York Moors are noted for their beauty – the 840 was declared Britain's most scenic bus route by Bus Users UK while the X93 was the tenth most scenic.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-6) The cyclists in the 2018 and 2019 [Tour de Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_Yorkshire "Tour de Yorkshire") passed through a section of the North York Moors.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-8) ## Physical geography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_York_Moors&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Physical geography")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Rj_north_york_moors.jpg/250px-Rj_north_york_moors.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rj_north_york_moors.jpg) Aerial photo of the North York Moors The North York Moors consist of a [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") plateau, dissected by a number of deep [dales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dale_(landform) "Dale (landform)") or valleys containing cultivated land or woodland. The largest dale is [Eskdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eskdale,_North_Yorkshire "Eskdale, North Yorkshire"), the valley of the [River Esk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Esk,_North_Yorkshire "River Esk, North Yorkshire") which flows from west to east and empties into the North Sea at [Whitby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitby "Whitby"). At the western end of Eskdale, the valley divides into three smaller dales, [Westerdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerdale "Westerdale") (the upper valley of the River Esk), [Baysdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baysdale "Baysdale") and [Commondale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commondale "Commondale").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-9) A series of side dales drain into Eskdale from the moorland on its southern side: from west to east these are [Danby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danby,_North_Yorkshire "Danby, North Yorkshire") Dale, [Little Fryup Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Fryup_Dale "Little Fryup Dale"), [Great Fryup Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fryup_Dale "Great Fryup Dale"), [Glaisdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaisdale "Glaisdale") and the [Goathland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goathland "Goathland") valley. [Kildale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kildale "Kildale"), west of Commondale and separated only by a low watershed, is drained by the [River Leven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Leven,_North_Yorkshire "River Leven, North Yorkshire"), which flows west to join the [River Tees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tees "River Tees"). The [Cleveland Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Hills "Cleveland Hills") rise north and west of Eskdale. They merge into the [Hambleton Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hambleton_Hills "Hambleton Hills"), which form the western edge of the North York Moors and form a sharp escarpment overlooking the [Vale of Mowbray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vale_of_Mowbray "Vale of Mowbray"). On their south side, the moorland is incised by a series of dales which cut through the [Tabular Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabular_Hills "Tabular Hills") to drain into tributaries of the [River Derwent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Derwent,_Yorkshire "River Derwent, Yorkshire"). The westernmost dale is [Rye Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rye_Dale "Rye Dale"), to the west of which rise the Hambleton Hills. [Bilsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilsdale "Bilsdale") is a side dale of Rye Dale. East of Bilsdale [Bransdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bransdale "Bransdale"), [Farndale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farndale "Farndale"), [Rosedale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosedale,_North_Yorkshire "Rosedale, North Yorkshire") and [Newton Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton_Dale "Newton Dale") cut into the moorland. In the south east, the landscape is marked by the narrow valleys of the upper reaches of the Derwent and its upper tributaries.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-10) About 22 per cent of the North York Moors is under woodland cover[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-DOI-1) (mostly located to the south-west and south-east), equivalent to more than 300 square kilometres of trees. It is home to the largest concentration of ancient and veteran trees in northern England.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-11) The Derwent crosses the Vale of Pickering flowing westwards, turns southwards at Malton and flows through the eastern part of the [Vale of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vale_of_York "Vale of York") before emptying into the [River Ouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Ouse,_Yorkshire "River Ouse, Yorkshire") at [Barmby on the Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barmby_on_the_Marsh "Barmby on the Marsh").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_York_Moors#cite_note-CAMS-12) ### Climate \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_York_Moors&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Climate")\] As part of the United Kingdom, the North York Moors area generally has warm summers and relatively mild winters. Weather conditions vary from day to day as well as from season to season. The latitude of the area means that it is influenced by predominantly westerly winds with [depressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(weather) "Depression (weather)") and their associated [fronts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_(weather) "Front (weather)"), bringing with them unsettled and windy weather, particularly in winter.
